title: Transverse Nature of Electromagnetic Waves
short_intro: Electromagnetic waves propagate through space via mutually perpendicular, oscillating electric and magnetic field vectors that are also perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. This intrinsic vector orientation confirms their purely transverse wave character.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the direction of electric field E, magnetic field B, and wave velocity c, along with basic right-hand rule applications and electromagnetic spectrum properties.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation from Maxwell's equations in free space, phase relationships between E and B, impedance of free space, and mathematical proof of transverse nature using divergence equations.

prerequisites: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral forms
Vector calculus identities and cross products

concept_notes.heading: Orthogonality of E, B, and Propagation Vector k
bullets: The electric field vector (E) and magnetic field vector (B) in an electromagnetic wave oscillate perpendicular to each other.
Both fields are strictly perpendicular to the direction of propagation given by the wave vector (k) or pointing vector direction.
The cross product E x B points precisely in the direction of energy propagation, which is the direction of the wave velocity c.

concept_notes.heading: Proof via Maxwell's Equations in Free Space
bullets: In charge-free and current-free space, Maxwell's curl equations govern the spatial and temporal variations of E and B.
Applying Faraday's law of induction (curl E = -dB/dt) forces the electric field to be perpendicular to the wave propagation vector.
Applying Ampere-Maxwell law (curl B = mu_0 epsilon_0 dE/dt) forces the magnetic field to be perpendicular to the wave propagation vector.

concept_notes.heading: Magnitude Ratio and Impedance of Free Space
bullets: The magnitude of the electric field and magnetic field are related by the constant wave speed: E = cB.
The ratio of the magnitudes of electric to magnetic field amplitudes equals the characteristic impedance of free space (Z_0 = sqrt(mu_0 / epsilon_0)).
The numerical value of the characteristic impedance of free space is approximately 376.7 ohms.

concept_notes.heading: Polarization and Transverse Verification
bullets: The transverse nature allows electromagnetic waves to exhibit polarization, where the electric field vector is restricted to a specific plane.
Passage through polaroids demonstrates extinction when transmission axes are perpendicular, confirming the transverse vector model.
Longitudinal electromagnetic waves do not exist in free space because zero divergence conditions rule out parallel field oscillations.

derivations.title: Derivation of Transverse Nature from Maxwell's Equations
derivations.conditions: Free space (rho = 0, J = 0), monochromatic plane wave traveling in z-direction
steps: Assume a plane wave solution where fields depend only on z and t: E(z,t) = E_0 exp(i(kz - omega t)) and B(z,t) = B_0 exp(i(kz - omega t)).

Evaluate Faraday's law: curl E = - partial B / partial t. The curl operation for a z-dependent field yields (partial E_y / partial z) hat{x} - (partial E_x / partial z) hat{y} = - partial B / partial t.
Equating components shows that partial E_z / partial z = 0, which implies the longitudinal component of E has no spatial wave dependence and can be set to zero for traveling waves.
Similarly, apply Ampere-Maxwell law: curl B = mu_0 epsilon_0 partial E / partial t, which establishes that B_z = 0.
Conclusion: Both E_z and B_z vanish along the direction of propagation (z-axis), proving that E and B have only transverse components (x and y).
derivations.result: E_z = 0 and B_z = 0, proving the purely transverse nature of electromagnetic waves.

derivations.title: Derivation of Wave Equation and Field Amplitude Ratio
steps: Take the curl of Faraday's equation: curl(curl E) = - partial / partial t (curl B).
Use the vector identity curl(curl E) = grad(div E) - nabla^2 E. Since div E = 0 in free space, this simplifies to - nabla^2 E.
Substitute Ampere-Maxwell equation for curl B: - nabla^2 E = - mu_0 epsilon_0 partial^2 E / partial t^2.
Obtain the standard wave equation: nabla^2 E = mu_0 epsilon_0 partial^2 E / partial t^2, identifying wave speed c = 1 / sqrt(mu_0 epsilon_0).
Substitute harmonic forms into Faraday's equation to find k E_0 = omega B_0, leading to E_0 / B_0 = omega / k = c.
derivations.result: E_0 / B_0 = c and c = 1 / sqrt{mu_0 epsilon_0}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Orthogonal Sinusoidal Oscillations of E and B
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A 3D coordinate system showing propagation along the z-axis, electric field oscillations in the x-z plane (sine wave), and magnetic field oscillations in the y-z plane (cosine wave, phase-locked with E).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visually demonstrates that E and B are mutually perpendicular at every point and both are perpendicular to the direction of energy transport (z-axis).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT multiple-choice questions to identify field orientations when wave propagation direction is given.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Malus Law / Polarization Verification Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A source of unpolarized light passing through a polarizer (P1) and an analyzer (P2) rotated at angle 	heta, showing transmitted intensity variation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the transverse nature of waves because longitudinal waves would show no extinction when the analyzer is rotated.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual questions on why longitudinal waves (like sound waves in fluids) cannot be polarized.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hertz's Electromagnetic Wave Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An induction coil connected to spark gap transmitter spheres and a resonant wire loop receiver with a microscopic spark gap.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proved the existence of electromagnetic waves and showed spark generation depends on the orientation of the receiving loop relative to the electric field vector.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Historical and conceptual context for transverse wave detection and spark resonance.

solved_numericals.question: The magnetic field amplitude in an electromagnetic wave is B_0 = 3 	imes 10^{-8} T. What is the amplitude of the electric field E_0?
solution_steps: Recall the relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes: E_0 = c B_0.
Substitute the speed of light c = 3 	imes 10^8 m/s and B_0 = 3 	imes 10^{-8} T.
Calculate: E_0 = (3 	imes 10^8) 	imes (3 	imes 10^{-8}) = 9 V/m.

solved_numericals.question: A plane electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum along the x-direction. If the electric field is given by E_y = 100 cos(10^7 t - kx) V/m, calculate the propagation constant k, the frequency f, and the expression for the associated magnetic field B_z.
solution_steps: Identify the angular frequency omega from the given phase: omega = 10^7 rad/s.
Calculate propagation constant k = omega / c = 10^7 / (3 	imes 10^8) = 1/30 rad/m approx 0.033 rad/m.
Find magnetic field amplitude B_0 = E_0 / c = 100 / (3 	imes 10^8) = 3.33 	imes 10^{-7} T.
Write the magnetic field vector equation respecting the right-hand rule (E x B points along +x): B_z(x,t) = 3.33 	imes 10^{-7} cos(10^7 t - 0.033 x) Tesla.

solved_numericals.question: Find the average intensity (energy per unit area per unit time) of an electromagnetic wave in free space if the peak value of the electric field is 120 V/m. Given epsilon_0 = 8.85 	imes 10^{-12} C^2/N cdot m^2 and c = 3 	imes 10^8 m/s.
solution_steps: Use the intensity formula for electromagnetic waves: I = (1/2) c epsilon_0 E_0^2.
Substitute the given values: c = 3 	imes 10^8, epsilon_0 = 8.85 	imes 10^{-12}, E_0 = 120.
Multiply: I = 0.5 	imes (3 	imes 10^8) 	imes (8.85 	imes 10^{-12}) 	imes 14400.
Evaluate numerical product: I = 0.5 	imes 3 	imes 8.85 	imes 1.44 = 19.116 W/m^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes propagation in ideal isotropic, homogeneous, charge-free, and current-free free space unless stated otherwise.
Derivations of transverse nature assume plane wave approximations where wavefronts are infinite planes perpendicular to the propagation vector.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electromagnetic waves have longitudinal electric field components along the direction of travel.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electromagnetic waves in free space are purely transverse; both E and B vectors are strictly perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
common_misconceptions.why: Maxwell's divergence equations in free space (div E = 0 and div B = 0) mathematically eliminate any longitudinal field components.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The electric field and magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave are out of phase.
common_misconceptions.correct: E and B oscillate in phase with each other in a propagating plane electromagnetic wave.
common_misconceptions.why: The spatial and temporal derivatives in Maxwell's curl equations link them such that maximum E corresponds directly to maximum B at the same point in space and time.

quick_revision: E and B fields are mutually perpendicular and both are perpendicular to wave velocity c (E x B points along c).
Amplitude ratio is always E_0 / B_0 = c.
Free space impedance Z_0 = sqrt(mu_0 / epsilon_0) approx 376.7 Omega.
Sound waves are longitudinal and cannot be polarized, whereas light and EM waves are transverse and polarizable.
